---
title: "What a doctorate asks of you"
last-reviewed: "2026-08-28"
---

You may be only weeks into the doctorate and already comparing a rough note with the polished thesis you hope to submit years from now. That comparison makes almost any early work look inadequate. The useful question is smaller: what does this piece of work need to do now? A private thinking note, a draft for supervision, an ethics application and a thesis claim do not need the same finish. This chapter helps you choose the right standard, expose the important uncertainty and take the next defensible step without pretending the work is complete.

## Judge the work by its current job

A doctorate asks you to make and defend an original contribution through research. It does not ask you to begin as an independent expert or to produce a flawless version of the thesis in your first year.

Official descriptions differ in wording and jurisdiction, but they converge on several features: advanced knowledge, original research or application, critical judgement, responsible conduct, and the ability to communicate and defend the work. The UK Quality Assurance Agency, for example, describes original contribution as common across research, professional, practice-based and practice-led doctorates [@qaa-doctoral-2020]. Australia places doctoral qualifications at Level 10 of its qualifications framework, but the precise award requirements are still set by the enrolling institution [@aqf-review-2019].

Your practical task is therefore to build a defensible chain:

> question → decision → method → evidence → interpretation → contribution

Every link will change as you learn. The standard is not “unchanging”. The standard is “traceable and defensible for the decision being made now”.

## What you need to decide

At any point in candidature, ask:

1. What decision or claim am I working on?
2. What standard applies at this stage?
3. What evidence is enough to move to the next stage without hiding a serious risk?

This prevents two common mistakes. The first is treating an early idea as though it must already meet the standard of an examined thesis. The second is calling weak work “good enough” without naming its purpose, risks or limitations.

::: {.decision-card}
**Smallest useful next action:** Write one sentence for each of these prompts: “The decision is…”, “The evidence I have is…”, “The main uncertainty is…”, and “The next check is…”.
:::

## Four different standards

“Good enough” changes with the purpose of the work. Use the correct threshold.

| Work state | What it is for | A proportionate standard |
|---|---|---|
| Exploratory note | Thinking privately | Clear enough that you can recover the idea and its source |
| Supervisor discussion draft | Getting diagnostic feedback | Complete enough to expose the decision, reasoning and uncertainty |
| Approval or governance document | Obtaining formal permission | Accurate, complete and compliant with the responsible body's current requirements |
| Thesis or publication claim | Entering the scholarly record | Supported, transparent, appropriately qualified and able to withstand review |

Do not use a low-risk drafting standard for ethics, safety, consent, privacy or integrity decisions. Those are stop points: the applicable approval or specialist advice comes before the activity.

## A practical way forward

### 1. Name the object

Avoid “work on the PhD”. Name the object you can inspect: a question map, search log, sampling rationale, analysis plan, figure, argument outline or decision record.

### 2. Name the use

A rough map for a supervision discussion and a protocol for formal approval have different audiences and consequences. State who will use the work and what decision it supports.

### 3. Define the present threshold

Use observable criteria. “Ready for discussion when the question, assumptions and two realistic options are visible” is testable. “Make it better” is not.

### 4. Test the main failure

Ask what could make the next step unsafe, invalid or wasteful. Check that issue first. A polished introduction does not rescue an infeasible recruitment plan.

### 5. Record the decision

Capture what was decided, why, by whom, what remains uncertain, and when it will be reviewed. The record protects learning when the project changes.

### 6. Move or escalate

Proceed when the threshold is met. Escalate when the uncertainty concerns approval, participant welfare, legal obligations, research integrity, safety, irrecoverable data loss or a change to the agreed candidature.

## Example: “Is my question ready?”

**Initial thought:** “I want to study why students disengage.”

**Present use:** A first supervision discussion, not an ethics submission.

**Threshold for discussion:** The population, phenomenon and intended contribution are visible; major assumptions are listed; at least two plausible ways to investigate the question have been considered.

**Evidence available:** A preliminary search, a short map of competing explanations and access to one relevant setting.

**Main uncertainty:** “Disengagement” may refer to attendance, participation, persistence or a subjective experience.

**Decision:** Take a one-page concept map and three candidate definitions to supervision. Do not select measures or draft participant material yet.

This is good enough for the conversation because it exposes the consequential uncertainty. It is not good enough for study approval or data collection.

## Traps that make the doctorate feel impossible

- **Trying to prove the whole thesis at once.** Convert the distant outcome into the next reviewable object.
- **Mistaking polish for readiness.** Test the reasoning and risk before formatting.
- **Treating a proposal as a contract with the future.** Preserve the rationale, then revise it when evidence changes.
- **Asking for feedback on an unnamed problem.** Tell the reviewer what decision you need help making.
- **Collecting information without a stopping rule.** Define what new information could change the decision.
- **Copying another project’s method.** Similar topics do not guarantee similar questions, constraints or valid inferences.
- **Using local convention as universal truth.** Label the source and jurisdiction of every formal requirement.
- **Waiting for confidence.** Seek enough evidence for a reversible next step, not a feeling of certainty.

## A quick check before you call it ready

Use this as a **do-confirm** check at a handover, submission or decision point. It adapts the handbook’s checklist design principles from Gawande and the WHO implementation guidance: few critical checks, a defined pause point, and local adaptation rather than an exhaustive task list [@gawande2010checklist; @who2009checklist].

- [ ] I can name the decision or use this work supports.
- [ ] I have applied the standard for this stage, not a later or easier one.
- [ ] The evidence, assumptions and unresolved uncertainty are visible.
- [ ] I have checked the failure that would make the next step unsafe or wasteful.
- [ ] Any required approval or specialist check occurs before the activity.
- [ ] The decision, owner and next review point will be recorded.

**Stop condition:** Do not proceed merely because a deadline is close if approval, participant welfare, integrity, safety or irreversible loss remains unresolved.

## Take a proposed decision to supervision

Bring:

1. the object you want reviewed;
2. the purpose and present threshold;
3. what you checked;
4. the strongest evidence and main uncertainty;
5. your provisional recommendation; and
6. one precise request, such as “Please tell me whether this is ready for a pilot, and identify the one issue that would block it.”

This turns supervision from “Is this okay?” into a decision-focused review.

## What differs across projects

Doctoral forms vary. A monograph, thesis by publication, creative practice doctorate, professional doctorate and industry-linked doctorate can express contribution differently. Part-time, remote, interdisciplinary and collaborative candidature also changes the rhythm and ownership of decisions. The common requirement to make a defensible contribution does not erase those differences.


## If you are stuck

- If you cannot identify the decision, use the [I’m stuck pathway](../../stuck/index.qmd).
- If the project feels too large, move next to [Day one to day 90](02-first-90-days.qmd) and build the minimum working system.
- If you cannot state the project’s possible contribution, use [Problem, gap and contribution](../part-03/07-problem-gap-contribution.qmd).
- If “good enough” has become perfectionism or avoidance, use [Technical failure and perfectionism](../part-11/32-technical-failure-perfectionism.qmd).

## Sources and limits

The qualification sources support the broad description of doctoral outcomes, not a universal examination rubric. The checklist sources support the design of pause-point checks, not the substantive requirements of research governance. Local rules and case-specific specialist advice take priority where required.
